name: Mbo (Democratic Republic of Congo)
confidence_why: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Rasmussen, Kent. 2018. A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington (Linguistics & TESOL Dissertations 116). xxviii+278 pp.
catalog_locator: p. 23, sec. 2.1.4 'Tone and Register'; then p. 142 and p. 143, sec. 4.4 'Summary Comparison of Mbo [zmw] verb root classes by tone'
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Rasmussen, Kent. 2018. A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington (Linguistics & TESOL Dissertations 116). xxviii+278 pp. Ch. 4 'Mbo [zmw]' pp. 121-146; Appendix C pp. 241-250.
tone_statements.quote: Available Mbo data vary somewhat from the Ndaka data presented in Chapter 3, but mostly in detail; we see the same basic story of three verb root classes by tone, each with a set of infinitive and conjugated tone melodies as in Table 23 ... the data clearly show three distinct verb root classes by tone, by both infinitive and conjugated tone patterns. ... For Mbo, bound subject pronouns are no longer segmentally unique. Pronouns for 2s and 3s are segmentally identical (both ∅) ... Mbo cannot use segmental material to distinguish 2s and 3s forms; this can only be done with tone.
tone_statements.summary: Verb roots in 3 lexical tone classes (Low/High/Rising), melodies in H/L pitch letters; no toneme count stated for Mbo. 'Downstep' = register drop per new L (automatic), plus a possible extra register shift in futures.

sources.note: Nothing for Mbo. First-hand verb-tone study (own fieldwork at Nyanya/Nia-Nia 2006, 2014, 2016): three Mbo verb root classes by tone (Low/High/Rising) with infinitive and conjugated pitch melodies (Table 23 p. 122), pitch traces, consonant-tone interaction (Table 27 p. 144); Appendix C: Mbo 2s vs 3s subject prefixes distinguished by tone alone. a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/penult: the sole word-stress remark (p. 116, sec. 3.5.4, 'penultimate word stress') concerns Ndaka [ndk], not Mbo; Mbo pitch remarks (pp. 129, 138) only say the High/Low and High/Rising contrasts in 2s-pas…

sources.citation: Kutsch Lojenga, Constance. 2003. Bila (D32). In Nurse & Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 450-474. London: Routledge. pp. 451-452 + fn. 3.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Phonology section is on Bila only. Mbo is grouped with Budu, Ndaka, Nyali, Vanuma (nine vowels with ATR harmony, reduced noun-class system) on lexical grounds; fn. 3: for Ndaka and Mbo 'phonological and morphological information is not yet available'. Nothing on Mbo stress.
